semantic_layer.text: Chapter 20: Current, Resistance, Ohm’s Law, Power, AC/DC

semantic_layer.detailed_figure_description: Hand-drawn simple circuit consisting of a battery on the left connected by a rectangular wire loop. The battery’s upper terminal is marked positive and its lower terminal negative; an orange V labels the voltage. Blue arrows marked I show conventional current moving clockwise around the loop. Black arrows and e⁻ labels show electrons moving in the opposite direction, counterclockwise, including downward through the battery.
semantic_layer.figure_alternative: Diagram of a battery circuit contrasting clockwise conventional current with counterclockwise electron flow.

semantic_layer.text: Electrical current (I) is the rate of flow of positive charge.

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: I equals Q divided by delta t, which equals Q divided by t.

semantic_layer.text: It’s direction (from DC, or direct current, voltage) is opposite the “flow” of electrons: from + to −.

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: The unit of amperes equals coulombs per second.

semantic_layer.text: A steady current of 2.5 A is created in a wire for 1.0 minute. How much charge passed by any given point, and how many electrons would this be?

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: I equals Q divided by delta t; therefore I equals 2.5 coulombs per second, which equals Q divided by t.
Q equals I times t, which equals 2.5 coulombs per second times 60 seconds, or 150 coulombs.
N equals 150 coulombs times one electron per 1.6 times 10 to the negative 19 coulombs, which equals 9.4 times 10 to the 20 electrons.
n equals 9.4 times 10 to the 20 electrons times one divided by 6.022 times 10 to the 23 electrons per mole, which equals 0.0016 mole.

semantic_layer.detailed_figure_description: A closed rectangular circuit has a battery on the left labeled V, with its positive terminal marked, and a zigzag resistor on the right labeled R in orange. Electron symbols, e⁻, and arrows around the wire show electron motion from the battery along the bottom toward the right, upward past the resistor, leftward across the top, and downward toward the battery.
semantic_layer.figure_alternative: Closed battery-and-resistor circuit showing electron flow around the wire.
The resistor circuit symbol: R followed by a zigzag line. An arrow labels it “circuit symbol.”

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: The units of ohms equal volts per ampere, which equal joules per coulomb divided by coulombs per second.

semantic_layer.text: A resistor resists the flow of current.
They're often used to limit current in a part of a circuit. Wires themselves have some resistance, but we'll usually ignore it.

semantic_layer.figure_alternative: Photograph of a green circuit board populated with many resistors and other components. Two handwritten arrows point to groups of components and are each labeled “resistors!”.

semantic_layer.detailed_figure_description: The upper sketch shows four electron-labeled blocks on a rough horizontal surface. An applied force F points right, while an orange friction force f points left. The lower sketch represents a cylindrical resistor: conventional current I points to the right through it, its length is labeled L, and a vertical bracket at the right is labeled A for cross-sectional area.
semantic_layer.figure_alternative: Two-part analogy comparing electron motion opposed by friction with current through a resistor of length L and cross-sectional area A.

semantic_layer.text: E⃗ fields in materials interact with current?

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: R is proportional to L over A; therefore, R equals rho times L over A.
Ohms equals ohm-meters times meters per square meter.

Resistivity depends on temperature — usually in metals

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: Current equals voltage divided by resistance.
Current equals one over resistance times voltage.

semantic_layer.detailed_figure_description: A coordinate graph has current I on the vertical axis and voltage V on the horizontal axis. Two blue straight lines pass through the origin with positive slopes; one is steep and the other is shallow. The graph illustrates that an ohmic material has a linear current-voltage relationship and that increasing resistance decreases the slope.

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: As resistance increases, the change in current divided by the change in voltage decreases.
Voltage equals current times resistance.

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: Voltage equals current times resistance, so the voltage at A is greater than the voltage at B.

semantic_layer.text: We say that “voltage drops” across a resistor.
The current is the same at A and B!
The current is lower through this whole circuit due to the resistor.

semantic_layer.detailed_figure_description: A closed circuit is drawn as a loop crowded with small rectangular blocks labeled e⁻, representing electrons. At the top of the loop, the blocks pass through a zigzag resistor labeled R, illustrating a traffic-jam mental model. A battery at the bottom is labeled V, with a magenta plus sign on the left and a blue minus sign on the right.
semantic_layer.figure_alternative: Traffic-jam model of electrons crowded around a closed circuit containing resistor R and voltage source V.

semantic_layer.text: A flashlight bulb draws 300 mA from its 1.5 V battery. What’s the resistance of the bulb? If the battery degrades and only produces 1.2 V how would the current change?

semantic_layer.figure_alternative: Drawing of a lit flashlight with a bulb and two batteries inside its casing.

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: Current equals voltage divided by resistance. Therefore, resistance equals voltage divided by current, which equals 1.5 volts divided by 0.30 amperes, or 5.0 ohms.
When the voltage changes to 1.2 volts, current equals 1.2 volts divided by 5.0 ohms, which is 0.24 amperes, or 240 milliamperes.

semantic_layer.text: Suppose you want to connect your stereo to remote speakers. (a) If each wire must be 20 m long, what diameter copper wire should you use to keep the resistance less than 0.10 Ω per wire? (b) If the current to each speaker is 4.0 A, what is the potential difference, or voltage drop, across each wire?

semantic_layer.figure_alternative: Illustration of a stereo connected to two remote speakers. Each speaker is connected by a wire labeled 20 m.
Circuit schematic showing a voltage source V driving current I around a loop through the resistance R of the wiring and a speaker. Current arrows point clockwise.

semantic_layer.normalized_math: \text{(a)}\quad \rho_{\mathrm{Cu}}=1.68\times10^{-9}\ \Omega\cdot\mathrm{m},\qquad L=20\ \mathrm{m},\qquad R=0.10\ \Omega;\quad A=\pi r^2=\pi\left(\frac d2\right)^2;\quad R=\rho\frac{L}{A}=\frac{4\rho L}{\pi d^2}
semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: Part a. The resistivity of copper equals 1.68 times 10 to the negative 9 ohm meters. L equals 20 meters, and R equals 0.10 ohm. Area equals pi r squared, which equals pi times d over 2 squared. Resistance equals rho L over A, which equals 4 rho L over pi d squared.

Therefore d squared is greater than 4 rho L over pi R, so d is greater than the square root of 4 rho L over pi R. Substitution using 1.68 times 10 to the negative 8 ohm meters, 20 meters, and 0.10 ohm gives 2.1 millimeters.

Part b. V equals I R, which equals 4.0 amperes times 0.10 ohm. Therefore the voltage across the resistance is 0.400 volt, or 400 millivolts. Unit annotations identify amperes as coulombs per second and ohms as volts per ampere.
Power equals energy divided by time.
U equals q V.
Power equals charge times voltage divided by time, which equals current times voltage.
Power equals current times voltage.

warnings.message: The stated copper resistivity in part (a) appears as 1.68 × 10^-9 Ω·m, but the numerical substitution on the following line uses 1.68 × 10^-8 Ω·m.

Part (b) is positioned above part (a), creating a conflict between spatial top-to-bottom order and the semantic order indicated by the part labels. The nodes are ordered semantically as (a) followed by (b).

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: The unit of amperes equals coulombs per second.
The unit of volts equals joules per coulomb.
The unit of watts equals joules per second.
The unit of ohms equals volts per ampere, which equals volt-seconds per coulomb, which equals joule-seconds per coulomb squared.
Watts equal amperes times volts, equal coulombs per second times joules per coulomb, equal joules per second.
Using V equals I R, power equals I times I R, which equals I squared R.
Using I equals V over R, power equals V over R times V, which equals V squared over R.
Power equals current times voltage.
Power equals current squared times resistance.
Power equals voltage squared divided by resistance.

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: V equals V sub zero times sine of omega t.
Omega equals two pi f.
Sixty cycles per second times two pi radians per cycle equals three hundred seventy-seven radians per second.

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: V R M S equals the square root of the average of V squared.

semantic_layer.text: FACT: the average value of sin² θ (or cos² θ) over a cycle is 1/2.

semantic_layer.figure_alternative: Hand-drawn graph with vertical axis y, horizontal axis t, and a vertical value marker at 1. A sequence of rounded, mostly nonnegative humps begins at zero and is labeled “Sin(ωt).”

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: The average of sine squared of omega t equals one half.

V R M S equals the square root of the average of V sub zero squared times sine squared of omega t, which equals the square root of V sub zero squared times one half, which equals V sub zero divided by the square root of two.
V R M S equals V sub zero divided by the square root of two.

warnings.message: The graph is visibly labeled “Sin(ωt),” but its repeated mostly nonnegative humps and the surrounding discussion of sin² suggest that “sin²(ωt)” may have been intended. The visible label has been preserved.

semantic_layer.spoken_math_alternative: I equals V over R, which implies I equals V naught over R times sine of omega t.
I equals I naught times sine of omega t.
I naught equals V naught over R, the peak current.
I R M S equals one over the square root of two times I naught.
Average power equals R M S current times R M S voltage.
Average power equals R M S current squared times R.
Average power equals R M S voltage squared over R.

semantic_layer.text: Electrical power produces heat → too much produces fires / burns / melting etc...
A short is when there’s an unplanned low-resistance path in a circuit.
